questions.question: For a real normed vector space $V$ with distance $d(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v})=\|\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{v}\|$, which condition is the definition of $V$ being a Banach space?
options: A normed space is Banach if and only if every bounded sequence in it converges.
A normed space is Banach if and only if every convergent sequence in it is Cauchy.
A normed space is Banach if and only if every Cauchy sequence in it is bounded.
A normed space is Banach if and only if every Cauchy sequence converges within it.

questions.question: Which of these metric spaces is complete for the distance $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ restricted to the stated set?
options: $\mathbb{Q}$.
$\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$.
$\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Let $X$ be a subset of a metric space $(Y,d)$, with the distance $d$ restricted to $X$. Which observation proves that $X$ is not complete?
options: Some sequence in $X$ has no convergent subsequence in $X$.
Every Cauchy sequence in $X$ is bounded.
A Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges in $Y$ to a point outside $X$.
Some bounded sequence in $X$ is not Cauchy.

questions.question: Equip $X=(0,1)$ with $d(x,y)=|x-y|$. The sequence $x_n=1/n$, $n\ge2$, is Cauchy and converges to $0$ in $\mathbb{R}$. What does this show about $X$?
options: $X$ is not complete, because this Cauchy sequence has no limit in $X$.
$X$ is complete, because this sequence is bounded in $X$.
$X$ is complete, because all terms of this sequence belong to $X$.
$X$ is not complete, because this sequence is not Cauchy in $X$.

questions.question: Which condition is the definition of a metric space $(X,d)$ being complete?
options: Every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges to a point of $X$.
Every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges in some larger metric space containing $X$.
Every convergent sequence in $X$ is a Cauchy sequence.
Every sequence in $X$ converges to a point of $X$.

questions.question: Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space and $(x_n)$ a sequence in $X$. Which statement is true?
options: $(x_n)$ converges in $X$ if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.
$(x_n)$ converges in $X$ if and only if it is bounded.
$(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence if and only if it is eventually constant.
$(x_n)$ converges in $X$ if it is Cauchy, but a convergent sequence need not be Cauchy.

questions.question: Equip $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the discrete metric, $d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=1$ for $\boldsymbol{x}\neq\boldsymbol{y}$ and $d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x})=0$. Is this metric space complete?
options: Yes: a Cauchy sequence is eventually constant, so it converges to that constant value.
No: $(1/n,0,\dots,0)_{n\ge1}$ is a Cauchy sequence for $d$ without a limit for $d$.
Yes: $d$ is bounded by $1$, so every bounded sequence converges for $d$.
No: a sequence converges for $d$ only if it is constant, so most Cauchy sequences have no limit.

questions.question: Let $(V,\|\cdot\|)$ be a real normed vector space, and let $d$ be a complete metric on $V$. Which condition makes completeness of $d$ directly prove that $V$ is a Banach space for the given norm?
options: The metric $d$ is bounded on $V\times V$.
$d(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v})=\|\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{v}\|$ for all $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in V$.
$d(\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{v}+\boldsymbol{w})=d(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v})$ for all $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}\in V$.
$d(\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v})\ge\|\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{v}\|$ for all $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in V$.

questions.question: On $I=(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ take the usual distance $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ and the metric $d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|$. A sequence in $I$ converges for $d$ exactly when it converges for $d_{\tan}$, with the same limit. Which statement about completeness is correct?
options: Both $(I,d)$ and $(I,d_{\tan})$ are complete, since they have the same convergent sequences.
$(I,d_{\tan})$ is complete, but $(I,d)$ is not.
$(I,d)$ is complete, but $(I,d_{\tan})$ is not.
Neither is complete, since $I$ is an open interval.

questions.question: Let $P$ be the vector space of real polynomial functions on $[0,1]$, with the uniform norm $\|p\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|p(x)|$. Is $(P,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ a Banach space?
options: Yes: it is a normed vector space with the uniform norm, so it is a Banach space.
Yes: it lies inside the bounded functions on $[0,1]$, which form a Banach space.
No: the Taylor polynomials of $\mathrm{e}^x$ at $0$ are Cauchy, but their uniform limit $\mathrm{e}^x$ is not a polynomial.
Yes: by the Weierstrass approximation theorem, every continuous function on $[0,1]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.
